scenarios.title: Recover behind the puck-side handoff
scenarios.objective: Track the second attacker after a puck-side handoff and keep the net-side lane in view.
scenarios.briefing: Gold attacks the Navy net. Gold 1 carries toward the Navy net, D1 is set near that route, and Gold 2 is inside support. YOU is recovering between the puck side and Gold 2; C trails farther back.
cues: D1 is set on the puck-side route.

questions.prompt: Which two checks shape your recovery?

questions.prompt: Arrange a recovery update.

options.text: Locate the carrier and inside support
Choose the more dangerous reachable lane
Call the new assignment and scan again

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a net-side relationship with Gold 2 while keeping D1 visible.

questions.prompt: Gold 2 cuts inside behind D1. What deserves the quickest re-read?

options.text: The inside lane and whether D1 needs help
Stay with the original recovery line
Follow C because C is trailing

questions.explanation: The inside cut changes the danger; support D1 or recover to that lane according to the visible route.

questions.prompt: What makes a recovery call useful after a puck-side handoff?
questions.explanation: Name the covered carrier, the inside attacker and the lane you are taking. If either route changes, call the new threat before moving.

scenarios.title: Turn the forecheck into a support angle
scenarios.objective: Use a changing forecheck to select a reachable teammate and preserve a reset connection.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the Gold net. YOU owns the puck near the neutral-zone boards; Gold 1 closes the wall and Gold 2 shades F1. D2 is deeper across the rink, while F1 offers a forward connection.
cues: D2 is the deeper reset and F1 is ahead.

questions.prompt: Which two observations help choose a route?

options.text: Gold 1's pressure line
Whether F1 or D2 is reachable

questions.explanation: Pressure and reachability create the decision; the side of the rink alone is insufficient.

questions.prompt: Arrange the regroup scan.

options.text: Read the forecheck route
Compare F1 and D2
Carry or pass, then check the next lane

questions.explanation: The angle is selected after both pressure and support are located.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a central angle that keeps D2 and F1 visible.
questions.explanation: This opens a view of both the reset and forward connection without copying either player.

questions.prompt: Gold 2 steps toward F1 while Gold 1 stays wide. What is useful?

options.text: Protect the puck and compare D2 with the new inside lane
Force F1 because Gold 2 moved
Use D2 without checking the carrier angle

questions.explanation: The pressure picture changed, so the reset and forward options need a fresh comparison.

questions.prompt: Why does an angle help a regroup more than simply moving away from the boards?
questions.explanation: An angle can keep the puck carrier connected to both D2 and F1 while showing the forecheck. If one route closes, the other remains a live branch only when reachable.

scenarios.title: Call the net-side exchange
scenarios.objective: Coordinate a behind-net exchange by naming the puck carrier, inside threat and teammate cover.
scenarios.briefing: Gold attacks the Navy net. Gold 1 carries behind the Navy net; YOU is on the near side, D2 is opposite, and C protects the slot against Gold 2. The handoff depends on which side Gold 1 exits.
cues: Gold 1 is behind the Navy net.
YOU and D2 are on opposite sides.
C is the slot support against Gold 2.

scenarios.title: Stay above a low cycle
scenarios.objective: Maintain a separated high outlet while teammates cycle low in the attacking zone.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks Gold’s net. F1 carries behind the goal line; F2 supports along the side and YOU arrive high. Gold 1 guards the slot, Gold 2 watches the higher lane, and Gold 3 protects space near the net.
cues: F1 controls below the Gold net.

options.text: F1
F2
YOU

questions.explanation: The setup assigns the puck below the net to F1.

questions.prompt: Which two details support a high outlet?

options.text: F1's ability to see above support
Gold 1's slot coverage
Following F2 into the same low space

questions.explanation: Carrier visibility and the slot defender shape the value of a separated high outlet.

questions.prompt: Arrange a high-outlet read.

options.text: Locate F1, F2 and the slot defender
Offer a separated high lane
Re-check the carrier and point-side pressure

questions.explanation: The outlet remains useful only when the carrier and pressure can connect to it.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a high pocket away from F2 with F1 visible.
questions.explanation: This creates a different high connection while leaving the low cycle space open.

questions.prompt: Gold 1 leaves the slot to pressure the puck. What should YOU weigh?

options.text: An inside connection if F1 can reach it, or hold high if Gold 2 covers
Drop beside F2 without checking the slot
Shoot because the slot defender moved

questions.explanation: Gold 1 leaving can open an inside branch, but F1’s passing route and Gold 2’s coverage still need a scan.

questions.prompt: How does a high outlet help a low cycle?
questions.explanation: It gives F1 a separated option and can make Gold choose between the slot and the carrier. If the route is covered, remain available or reset instead of crowding F2.

cues: F1 is near the net-front lane.

rows.reason: F1 is the puck owner at (28,-5), beyond the Gold goal line on Navy's +x attack; the key correctly identifies F1. Gold 2/A2 and Gold 3/A3 are visible alternatives.
F1's ability to connect to a separated high outlet and Gold 1's slot coverage are both scene-grounded checks. Following F2 into the same low space is a credible crowding error.

The suggested order names the actual carrier F1, support F2 and the slot defender, then requires a fresh pressure read. The coaching basis and explanation make this a flexible routine rather than a mandatory scored ladder.
Reference (18,4.5) is a high pocket away from F2 at (22,-8), while F1 at (28,-5) remains a visible low carrier. It is an example support point with no claim of unique timing.

When Gold 1 leaves the slot, the keyed branch appropriately depends on F1's reachable inside route or Gold 2's coverage. Dropping into F2's low space or shooting automatically are credible alternatives.
The explanation ties the high outlet to F1's low cycle and Gold's choice while preserving a reset if the route closes. It adds learning beyond merely naming the carrier.
